system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 5 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2184-02-12 20:41:00 to 2184-02-17 16:48:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of mesenteric fibromatosis, chronic abdominal pain, and TPN dependence was admitted directly from GI clinic due to severe, uncontrolled pain and malnutrition after discontinuing home TPN for three weeks. She was restarted on hospital TPN with improved tolerance and nutritional support. Pain management was optimized through consultation with the chronic pain service, including a trial of Dilaudid PCA, followed by multiple medication adjustments, ultimately transitioning to methadone. A new left thigh hematoma was identified, associated with supratherapeutic anticoagulation from home Lovenox; it was managed conservatively with dose reduction to prophylactic levels, warm/cold compresses, and a lidocaine patch. Her nausea improved, anemia was monitored, and she remained stable without active bleeding or infection. She was discharged home with services on adjusted pain and anticoagulation regimens, new TPN formula, and follow-up plans.
problems: Chronic venous embolism and thrombosis of other specified veins

diffuse body aches, and erythematous line site, was treated with 
Vancomycin until the line was replaced by ___.

# Low-grade fever: It was documented at home, but pt was 
afebrile throughout the hospital stay. There were several 
possible sources of infection included line, pneumonia, urinary 
tract infections, bacteremia.  Pt was started on Vanc 
empirically.  It was decided that line infection was most likely 
especially because some purulent discharge was noted from the 
existing femoral line on presentation.  The IV access team 
recommended an MRV to assess pt's vasculature, however, there 
was concern whether it would be safe since the pt has had a 
dorsal column stimulator placed in her back in ___ for chronic 
pain.  After much investigation, it was discovered that MRI is 
not recommended with the particular device that was implanted in 
her.  Therefore, pt did not have an MRV.  The current left 
femoral line was taken out and another femoral line on the right 
was placed by Interventional Radiology.  All blood cultures were 
negative.  The catheter tip culture of the removed line was sent 
for culture, which was pending at time of discharge.  Vanc was 
discontinued on day of discharge.
.
# Nutrition: A regular diet as tolerated by patient.  Pt's TPN 
was on hold during the hospital stay due to concern for infected 
line.

was continued on home lovenox.
.
# Anemia: Hct was trended daily, which remained stable.  Pt was 
continued on home iron.

# Depression: Pt was continued on home psych regimen.  Pt was 
maintained on home trazodone prn, aripiprazole, lamotrigine.  
Psych was consulted to aid in our management of this pt who 
recommended frequent communication between the team and pt.

gabapentin, clonidine.  Also, pt was continued on a dilaudid PCA 
for additional pain control during hospital stay, with 
understanding that it will be suspended on discharge.

octreotide, misoprostol.

radiology_notes.text:
CLINICAL HISTORY:  ___ woman with fever.  Please evaluate for
pneumonia.

COMPARISON:  ___.

FINDINGS:  The lungs are clear.  Persistent elevation of the right
hemidiaphragm is unchanged.  Spinal stimulators are once again visualized. 
There are no pleural effusions.  There are no focal consolidations or
opacities worrisome for pneumonia.  Cardiomediastinal silhouette and hilar
contours are unremarkable.

HISTORY:  A ___ woman with suspected line infection.

OPERATORS:  Dr. ___ and Dr. ___ (attending)
performed the procedure.

ANESTHESIA:  Moderate sedation was provided by administering divided doses of
Dilaudid PCA and Versed throughout the total intraservice time of 30 minutes,
during which the patient's hemodynamic parameters were continuously monitored.
1 mg of Versed and 0.25 mg of Dilaudid were administered.

PROCEDURE:  Written informed consent was obtained from the patient after
explaining the risks, benefits and alternatives and the procedure to the
patient.  The patient was brought to the angio suite and laid supine on the
angio table.  Both the right and left groin were prepped and draped in a
sterile fashion.

Under ultrasound guidance, the right patent common femoral vein was accessed
with a micropuncture needle.  The 0.018 guidewire was inserted through the
needle and was imaged in the IVC via fluoroscopy.  Skin ___ was given and the
needle was exchanged for a micropuncture sheath.  Then, the inner dilator and
0.018 guidewire was exchanged for a ___.  The ___ was extended into the
IVC under fluoroscopic guidance.  After appropriate measurements were
performed with the tunnel, attention was directed to the right thigh.

Interdermal 1% lidocaine was given at the tunnel entrance site.  Then, a skin
___ was made with a scalpel and 1% lidocaine with epinephrine was injected in
the planned tunnel area.  Then, a tunnel was created using a tunneling device.
Once the catheter was out at the venotomy site, the micropuncture sheath was
exchanged for a #8 ___ dilator.  Once the tract was dilated with an
___ dilator, a ___ peel-away sheath was inserted.  Then, the
dilator and guidewire were removed and the catheter was fed into the IVC.  The
venotomy site was sutured with ___ Vicryl and the catheter was secured with 0
silk.  A StatLock was also applied to the line.  Sterile dressing was applied.

Sterile dressing was taken out from the left femoral catheter.  There was a
small amount of pus that was expressing from the tunnel.  The cuff of the
catheter was outside the tunnel.  The tunnel line was removed and pressure was
held for five minutes over the venotomy site.  There was no hemorrhage from
the line site.  Sterile dressing was applied

The patient tolerated the procedure well and did not have any immediate
complications.

IMPRESSION:
1.  Previous CTA and venogram findings showed central SVC stenosis and a
decision was taken to place a right femoral tunneled line.

2. Left femoral tunneled line removed and tip sent for culture.

3.  Uncomplicated insertion of the right common femoral double-lumen line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. I understand you came in with fever and chills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve had a low-grade fever at home, up to 100.1, and I’ve been feeling achy and sweaty. It feels just like my past line infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. We noticed some redness and a small amount of pus around your left femoral line. That’s definitely concerning. We’ve started you on IV vancomycin just in case.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. I’ve had these infections before—usually from the line. But I’m also nauseous and throwing up more than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We gave you some IV promethazine for the nausea. We’ll keep an eye on it. Your blood work shows your white count is normal, which is reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t been on my methadone lately—it wasn’t helping my pain. I’ve been using the Dilaudid PCA instead.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll continue your home pain meds—amitriptyline, gabapentin, clonidine—and keep the PCA for now. We’ll talk to the pain team about adjusting things if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. And please let the ID and pain services know I’m here. I’m on Lovenox too, for my history of clots.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Already done. We’re continuing your Lovenox. We’re also monitoring your hemoglobin—it’s stable so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had anemia for a while. I’m on iron. Is my TPN going to be paused?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re holding TPN for now because of the possible line infection. We don’t want to feed any bacteria. You can have regular food as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s fine. I can eat a little. But I’m worried—could this be serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re being cautious. The redness and pus suggest the line might be infected. We drew blood cultures and sent a catheter tip for testing once it’s removed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: When will that happen?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning to replace the line with a new one on the right side. But first, we wanted to check your veins with an MRV.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, I can’t have an MRI. I have a spinal stimulator for pain. They said it’s not safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re right—we confirmed that. So we’ll go ahead with replacing the line without the MRV. Interventional Radiology will place a new tunneled catheter in your right femoral vein.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s fine. I trust them. Will I be awake?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll get some sedation—Dilaudid and Versed—so you’ll be relaxed but may remember parts of it. It’s usually well tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your blood cultures came back negative so far. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. Any other tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your chest X-ray was clear—no pneumonia. We’re also watching your electrolytes and kidney function. Everything looks stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve felt a bit better today—no fever, and the nausea is less.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll keep the vancomycin going until after the line is replaced, just to be safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re scheduling the line replacement for tomorrow morning. Any questions before then?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will they remove the old line completely?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll remove the left femoral line and send the tip for culture. Then place the new one on the right.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my TPN—when can I restart?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll wait a few days after the new line is in and we’re sure there’s no infection. We don’t want to risk seeding the new line.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Understood. I’ll manage with food and IV fluids for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just checking in. You’re still doing well—no fever, labs stable. The procedure is set for tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. I’m feeling okay. A bit anxious about the procedure, but I know it’s necessary.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Totally normal. The team is experienced, and you’ll be sedated. We’ll be right there with you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. The procedure went smoothly. They removed the old line—there was a bit of pus in the tunnel—and placed the new one in your right groin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember some pressure, but not much pain. Is the old line being tested?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the tip was sent for culture. We’ll get results in a few days. For now, we’ll keep you on antibiotics until we’re confident it’s clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my pain meds? Can I keep the PCA?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, for now. But we’ll taper it off before discharge. We’ll keep your regular meds—amitriptyline, gabapentin, clonidine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’m glad we’re addressing the line. I’ve had too many infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re taking every precaution. The new site is clean, and we’ll teach you how to care for it at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—your catheter tip culture came back with no growth. No bacteria found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief! Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. We’ll stop the vancomycin since there’s no sign of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great. What about my TPN?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You can restart it at home through the new line. Be sure to follow your usual sterile technique.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And my other meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Back to your regular list—no changes. We’ve given you a printed copy. Continue Lovenox, pain meds, and everything else as before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I get fever or redness at the new site?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or go to the ER. Watch for redness, swelling, or drainage. Otherwise, follow up with your primary team in a week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you in follow-up if needed.

summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a complex history of sclerosing mesenteritis, chronic abdominal pain, TPN dependence via femoral catheter, and recurrent line infections was admitted for fever, chills, and erythema at her left femoral line site with purulent discharge. She was started on IV vancomycin for suspected catheter-related infection. Blood cultures were negative, and a chest X-ray showed no pneumonia. Due to contraindication from a spinal stimulator, an MRV was not performed. The infected left femoral catheter was removed and replaced with a new tunneled line in the right femoral vein. The catheter tip culture later showed no growth. TPN was held during admission and will be resumed at home. Antibiotics were discontinued at discharge. She remained afebrile, with stable labs and controlled symptoms. She was discharged home with instructions to monitor the new line site and resume her prior medication and TPN regimen.
